lessons.title: Lagrangian Duality: The Dual Problem and What It Tells You

children.text: Every tool so far has searched for the optimal weights directly. This final chapter introduces a different vantage point on the exact same problem: instead of asking which portfolio is best, ask what the multipliers themselves reveal when treated as the thing being optimized. This shift in perspective, called duality, is not just a curiosity. It is the theoretical foundation every real-world quadratic programming solver runs on.

body.text: Every constrained optimization problem has a shadow twin, built from the same Lagrangian, viewed from the multipliers' side instead of the decision variables' side. The twin's best value is always a bound on the original problem's best value, and for convex problems, the two meet exactly.

children.text: From the Lagrangian to the Dual Function

markDefs.definition: A new function, built by minimizing the Lagrangian over the original decision variables x, for fixed values of the multipliers. It depends only on the multipliers, never on x.

children.text: Take the exact same Lagrangian from Chapter 5, but instead of setting its gradient to zero, minimize it over x completely, for whatever multiplier values happen to be fixed. The result is called the

body.caption: The dual function: minimize the Lagrangian over x, treating lambda and nu as fixed constants.
The dual problem: maximize the dual function over the multipliers themselves.

body.text: The original problem, minimizing f(x) over portfolio weights subject to constraints, is now called the primal problem. Its dual is a completely different optimization problem: instead of searching over portfolio weights, it searches over multiplier values, and instead of minimizing, it maximizes. Same underlying Lagrangian, two different problems built from it.

children.text: Weak Duality: The Dual Is Always a Bound

body.latex: g(\boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\nu}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{for any feasible } \mathbf{x} \text{ and any } \boldsymbol{\lambda} \geq \mathbf{0}
body.caption: Weak duality. True for every optimization problem, convex or not.

children.text: The reasoning is short: since g minimizes the Lagrangian over every possible x, it is in particular no larger than the Lagrangian's value at any specific feasible x. And at a feasible x, every inequality term λi gi(x) is a non-negative multiplier times a non-positive number, so it cannot be positive, while every equality term vanishes outright since hj(x) = 0. Both effects only ever push the Lagrangian's value down toward f(x) or below it, never above. Weak duality needs nothing about convexity to hold, it is true unconditionally.

Weak duality only guarantees the dual's best value sits at or below the primal's best value, leaving a possible gap between them. For convex problems, the kind this entire course has built, under mild conditions that gap closes to exactly zero: the dual's maximum equals the primal's minimum, precisely. That result, called strong duality, is the next lesson's subject. This lesson closes with a worked example that shows it happening in practice, on a problem already solved three different ways earlier in this course.
Worked Example: The Dual of the Minimum Variance Problem

body.caption: The minimum variance Lagrangian, budget constraint only, from Chapter 4.
Minimizing the Lagrangian over w for a fixed nu, exactly Chapter 4's stationarity step.
Substituting w back into the Lagrangian and simplifying gives the dual function, purely in terms of nu.
Maximizing this simple downward parabola in nu, using plain unconstrained calculus from Chapter 3.

body.text: Plug in C ≈ 24.186, the Reliance-TCS value from Chapter 4, and nu* = 2/24.186 ≈ 0.0827, exactly the multiplier value computed there by a completely different route, and g(nu*) = 1/24.186 ≈ 0.04134, exactly the minimum variance value found in Chapter 3 by substitution and confirmed again in Chapter 4 by the Lagrangian. Maximizing the dual function landed on precisely the same number as minimizing the primal, this is strong duality actually happening, not just claimed.

body.title: Use weak duality as a certificate
body.question: You find a feasible portfolio x with objective value f(x) = 0.0435, and separately find dual-feasible multipliers with dual value g(λ, ν) = 0.0435, exactly matching. What can you conclude, using weak duality alone?
options: Nothing definitive; the two values matching is a coincidence
x is provably the optimal solution, since weak duality sandwiches the true optimal value between g(λ, ν) and f(x), and here they are equal
You need strong duality to conclude anything; weak duality alone is not enough
body.explanation: Weak duality guarantees g(λ, ν) ≤ f(x*) ≤ f(x) for the true optimal value f(x*), for any feasible x and any dual-feasible (λ, ν). If g(λ, ν) and f(x) happen to be exactly equal, f(x*) is sandwiched between two equal numbers, so it must equal both. This is a fully general certificate of optimality, valid even without first knowing the problem is convex.

body.title: Read a solver's stopping point
body.scenario: A solver reports it found a portfolio with variance 0.0413, and also reports a dual bound of 0.0412 at the point it stopped.
body.prompt: Using weak duality, what can you say about how far this portfolio might be from the true optimum, even without knowing the exact answer?
body.modelAnswer: By weak duality, the true minimum variance lies between the dual bound and the found solution's value, somewhere in the range 0.0412 to 0.0413. So the found portfolio is guaranteed to be within 0.0001 of the true optimum, regardless of how the solver got there. This gap between the current primal value and the current dual bound is exactly how practical solvers know when to stop iterating: once it is small enough, they can certify near-optimality without ever computing the true optimum directly.

cards.definition: The original constrained optimization problem, minimizing over the decision variables x.
g(λ, ν) = min over x of the Lagrangian, for fixed multipliers. Depends only on the multipliers.
Maximize the dual function over the multipliers, subject to λ ≥ 0. A different optimization problem built from the same Lagrangian.
g(λ, ν) ≤ f(x) for any feasible x and dual-feasible (λ, ν). Holds unconditionally, even for non-convex problems.
For convex problems under mild conditions, the primal minimum and dual maximum are exactly equal, no gap. Proven in the next lesson.

points: The dual function, g(λ, ν), is built by minimizing the Lagrangian over x for fixed multipliers, turning the multipliers into the new decision variables of a second, related problem.
The dual problem maximizes the dual function subject to λ ≥ 0, a genuinely different optimization problem from the original, primal one.
Weak duality, g(λ, ν) ≤ f(x), holds for any feasible x and dual-feasible multipliers, for any optimization problem at all, convex or not.

Working out the dual of the minimum variance problem gives g(ν) = ν - (C/4)ν², and maximizing it reproduces the exact multiplier and minimum variance value found by three different methods earlier in this course.
When a primal feasible value and a dual feasible value coincide exactly, that is a fully general certificate of optimality, and it is exactly how real solvers know when to stop.
The next lesson proves why this gap closes to exactly zero for convex problems, the class this entire course has been built around.
